identification.summary: CovertNetwork-1658 is Microsoft's name for a network of compromised small office/home office (SOHO) routers, mostly TP-Link, used to conduct highly evasive password spray attacks; it is also known as xlogin and Quad7 (7777) [S1]. It is infrastructure rather than an intrusion set: Microsoft assesses that multiple Chinese threat actors use the credentials it harvests, and specifically observed Storm-0940 doing so [S1].
identification.firstObserved: 2023-08 (Microsoft observed credential-theft intrusions enabled by the password spray activity from August 2023) [S1]. The Quad7 botnet was first publicly documented by independent researcher Gi7w0rm in October 2023 [S5].
identification.notes: The name CovertNetwork-1658 maps to the Quad7/7777/xlogin botnet [S1]. Sekoia describes five login clusters tied to the operators (alogin, xlogin, axlogin, rlogin, zylogin); Microsoft's name corresponds to the TP-Link-focused xlogin activity [S1][S3][S6]. The catalogue record lists ORB07 as an alias, but none of the sources reviewed state this mapping, so it is not asserted here. Storm-0940 is a separate Microsoft-tracked actor that consumes the credentials; do not merge the two [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Unattributed to a named organization. Microsoft assesses that a threat actor located in China established and maintains the network [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states this as an assessment without a stated confidence level, and notes a likely close working relationship with Storm-0940 [S1]. Sekoia told The Hacker News the operators are likely Chinese state-sponsored actors [S5], whereas Sekoia's earlier July 2024 analysis assessed possible long-term business email compromise cybercriminal activity rather than an APT, with attribution an open question [S2]. These are differing vendor views and are not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites same-day use of CovertNetwork-1658 credentials by Storm-0940 as evidence of a likely close working relationship [S1]. The public sources reviewed do not detail the evidence for China-based operation beyond Microsoft's assessment [S1].

objectives: Credential theft against Microsoft customers via low-volume password spraying, with the harvested credentials then used by Chinese threat actors for initial access [S1]. Sekoia also saw the operators' botnet used for brute-force attempts against Microsoft 365 accounts and, via the ASUS-linked alogin cluster, against VPN, SSH and Telnet services [S3][S5][S6].

targeting.notes: The spray itself targets many accounts at a given organization with very few attempts, and Microsoft describes the victims as multiple Microsoft customers [S1]. The sectors and regions above describe Storm-0940, the consumer of the credentials, not the botnet's own spray target list [S1]. Separately, the compromised router nodes are victims: Sekoia's infection counts were highest in Bulgaria, the US and Ukraine [S6]. The same operators expanded to ASUS routers, Zyxel VPNs, Ruckus routers and Axentra NAS devices [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft assesses the actor exploits a router vulnerability for remote code execution (specific exploit under investigation in 2024); post-compromise it downloads a Telnet binary and the xlogin backdoor from an FTP server, runs an access-controlled shell on TCP 7777 and a SOCKS5 server on TCP 11288 [S1]. About 8,000 devices were active on average, roughly 20 percent spraying at any time, with average node uptime of about 90 days and rotating IP addresses [S1]. In about 80 percent of cases only one sign-in attempt per account per day was made, defeating failure-count detection per IP or account [S1]. Team Cymru counted 12,783 active bots across the 7777 and 63256 groups in the 30 days to 2024-08-05 [S6]. Sekoia later observed a chain on TP-Link WR841N combining CVE-2023-50224 (credential file disclosure) and CVE-2025-9377 (Parental Control command injection), which works only if remote administration is exposed to the internet; CISA added CVE-2025-9377 to its KEV catalog per Malwarebytes [S7]. Sekoia also reported moves to new backdoors and reverse shells such as the UPDATE backdoor instead of SOCKS5 proxies [S6].

campaigns.name: Highly evasive password spray against Microsoft customers
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed intrusions that stole credentials from multiple customers enabled by password spray attacks from CovertNetwork-1658 [S1].

campaigns.name: Public documentation of Quad7
campaigns.summary: Researcher Gi7w0rm first publicly documented the botnet, then mainly TP-Link routers and Dahua DVRs [S5].

campaigns.name: Sekoia investigation of the 7777 botnet
campaigns.summary: Sekoia reported the operators relaying Microsoft 365 password spraying through compromised TP-Link routers and assessed possible BEC cybercrime; unique IPs fell from 16,000 (August 2022) to about 7,000 (July 2024) [S2].

campaigns.name: Team Cymru analysis and ASUS cluster
campaigns.summary: Team Cymru reported 12,783 bots across the 7777 and 63256 groups over 30 days to 2024-08-05 and a second ASUS-heavy cluster on port 63256 [S6].

campaigns.name: Operator expansion
campaigns.summary: Sekoia described five login clusters and expansion to Zyxel VPN, Ruckus routers and Axentra NAS, with new backdoors [S3][S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Microsoft publication and Storm-0940 link
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published CovertNetwork-1658 reporting, said usage of the original infrastructure declined substantially after the July and August vendor reports (Censys data, 2024-08-01 to 2024-10-29), and that the network was likely acquiring new infrastructure with modified fingerprints, citing increased recent activity [S1].

campaigns.name: TP-Link exploit chain and KEV listing
campaigns.summary: Sekoia analysis of a WR841N exploit chain (CVE-2023-50224 plus CVE-2025-9377); TP-Link urged owners of affected end-of-service models to update or replace devices [S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based operator of the network assessed by Microsoft, working closely with consumers such as Storm-0940 [S1]. Sekoia's views on actor type differ (BEC criminals versus likely state-sponsored) [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Router exploitation for RCE, xlogin backdoor, SOCKS5 relays, low-and-slow password spray with one attempt per account per day [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised SOHO routers, mostly TP-Link, with TCP 7777 shell and TCP 11288 SOCKS5; alogin ASUS cluster on 63256/63260; FTP server hosting tooling; rotating IPs, about 8,000 active nodes on average [S1][S6].
diamond.victim: Microsoft customer accounts sprayed for credentials, with Storm-0940 follow-on targets in North America and Europe; router owners are secondary victims [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Microsoft links credential use to Chinese actors targeting think tanks, government, NGOs, law firms and the defense industrial base [S1]. No further sociopolitical drivers are sourced.
diamond.technology: Microsoft Entra/Azure and Microsoft 365 authentication; SOHO routers (TP-Link, ASUS), Zyxel VPN, Ruckus, Axentra NAS [S1][S5][S6].

gaps: The specific router vulnerability exploited in 2023-2024 was described as under investigation by Microsoft [S1].
Evidence for China-based operation and the exact relationship to Storm-0940 and other consumers is not public beyond Microsoft's assessment [S1].
Vendors disagree on actor type (BEC criminal versus state-sponsored) [S2][S5].
The ORB07 alias in the catalogue record is not confirmed by any source reviewed; Mandiant ORB reporting was not found to mention it.
Primary Sekoia and Team Cymru pages and MITRE ATT&CK (campaign C0055) pages could not be fetched; they are cited via search-result summaries and press coverage, so details need validation.
Post-2024 scale and current status of the botnet are unknown; the 2025 reporting covers an exploit chain only [S7].
Exact publication dates for the Sekoia posts and Team Cymru post were inferred from Microsoft and press references.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the relevant environment is cloud identity (Microsoft 365/Entra) plus the commercial SOHO router population used as egress [S1]. Step 3: adversary strength is high stealth, not high volume, with about 8,000 rotating nodes and one attempt per account per day [S1]. MLCOA: continued low-volume sprays against DoD-adjacent and defense industrial base tenants, with stolen credentials used same-day by Storm-0940 for access and lateral movement [S1]. MDCOA: operators rebuild infrastructure with modified fingerprints on new device types (ASUS, Zyxel, Ruckus, NAS) and reach accounts lacking MFA [S1][S3][S5]. Candidate indicators: sign-in failures spread across many accounts from consumer ISP address space, the two user-agent strings Microsoft listed, and legacy authentication use [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: tenant owners should monitor identity logs for single-ISP password spray patterns and ingest Microsoft detections such as Defender XDR password spray alerts [S1]. Authorities: any response affecting commercial or foreign router infrastructure sits outside DODIN-A operator authority; coordinate via the cyber command chain and CISA/vendor channels. Mission assurance: enforce MFA or passwordless, disable legacy authentication, use Conditional Access, reset passwords of targeted accounts [S1]. Coordination: share indicators with defense industrial base partners, and advise personnel to patch or replace end-of-service home routers [S7].
